theory.intro: If you cut a shape into pieces and rearrange them into a different shape, the total area stays the same. This idea turns hard shapes into easy ones.
facts: Cutting and rearranging **preserves area** — no surface is added or lost.
A parallelogram can be cut and rearranged into a **rectangle** with the same base and height.
Two equal triangles can be joined to make a parallelogram or rectangle.
steps: Cut the shape into pieces (often along a straight line).
Move the pieces to form a simpler shape, such as a rectangle.
The area is unchanged, so find the area of the simpler shape.

foundation.solution_text:
Move the left triangular piece to the gap beside the sloping right edge.
Translate it to the right side.

\draw (0,0) rectangle (4.5,2.4);\draw[dashed] (3.3,0)--(4.5,2.4);\draw[->] (-0.9,1.2)--(-0.1,1.2);\node[above] at (2.25,2.4) {rectangle};

foundation.question_text: A shape has area $18\text{ cm}^{2}$. It is cut into two pieces and rearranged with no gaps or overlaps. What is the area of the new shape?
foundation.solution_text:
Cutting and rearranging neither adds nor removes surface.
The new area is $18\text{ cm}^{2}$.

foundation.question_text: A square is cut into four pieces. All four pieces are used to make a new shape without overlap. Does the area increase, decrease or stay the same?
foundation.solution_text:
Every original piece is still present once, with no overlap.
The area stays the same.

Piece $B$ is $2$ units by $1$ unit. Rotate it so it is $1$ unit by $2$ units, then place it beside piece $A$.
Move piece $B$.

\draw (0,0) rectangle (3,2);\draw[dashed] (2,0)--(2,2);\node at (2.5,1) {$B$};

development.question_text: Noah rearranges all the pieces of a $24\text{ cm}^{2}$ rectangle, but two pieces overlap by $3\text{ cm}^{2}$. What area is covered by the new arrangement?
development.solution_text:
The overlapped region is counted twice among the pieces but covered only once.
$24-3=21$
The arrangement covers $21\text{ cm}^{2}$.

development.question_text: A $35\text{ cm}^{2}$ shape is cut and rearranged, but a $4\text{ cm}^{2}$ gap is left inside the outline. What is the area of the pieces, and what is the area inside the outline?
development.solution_text:
The pieces still total $35\text{ cm}^{2}$.
The outline includes the uncovered gap: $35+4=39$.
The outline encloses $39\text{ cm}^{2}$.

Cut the $2$-by-$1$ block at the lower right from the rest.
Rotate it $90^{\circ}$ and translate it beside the remaining $3$-by-$2$ rectangle.
The pieces form a $4$-by-$2$ rectangle.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\draw[gray!30,very thin] (0,0) grid (4,2);\draw (0,0) rectangle (4,2);\draw[dashed] (3,0)--(3,2);
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

mastery.question_text: A $6$ by $4$ rectangle is cut along a diagonal. One triangular half is reflected across the diagonal. Explain why the total area of the two pieces remains $24$ square units even though their visible union is smaller.
mastery.solution_text:
Each triangular piece still has area $12$ square units, so the pieces total $12+12=24$ square units.
Their visible union covers only $12$ square units because the reflection places one exactly on top of the other.

mastery.question_text: A tangram uses seven pieces to make a square. A new design uses only six of the pieces with no overlaps. Can it have the same area as the square? Explain.
mastery.solution_text:
No. One piece has been omitted, so some surface area has been removed.
Using only six pieces gives a smaller total area than the seven-piece square.

mastery.question_text: Two students use all the same pieces. Ava makes a compact rectangle. Ben makes a long irregular shape with no gaps or overlaps. Compare their areas and justify your answer.
mastery.solution_text:
Their areas are equal.
Both arrangements use every piece exactly once, so changing position and orientation changes the outline but not the total area.
